Above 10 bar the gE rule (MHV1) would suit, but it has no set here. PR at 1698 kPa, a light gas with a polar liquid (Carbon dioxide + Methanol, Carbon dioxide + Water, Hydrogen + Methanol, Hydrogen + Water, Carbon monoxide + Methanol, Carbon monoxide + Water, Nitrogen + Methanol, Nitrogen + Water): above about 10 bar the method guide recommends a cubic equation with a gE mixing rule (rule 4 of docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md). CHEPTA's rule of that kind would be refused: PR + gE (MHV1): Methanol + Nitrogen, a light gas with a polar liquid, has no NRTL parameters fitted inside the rule (src/data/mhv1.json) and none in the databank, so its solubility would rest on no data (proposal 0018). Pairs fitted so far: carbon-dioxide + methanol, hydrogen + methanol, carbon-monoxide + methanol, methane + methanol, carbon-dioxide + water, hydrogen + water, carbon-monoxide + water, methane + water. Give the pair's NRTL parameters in mixing.nrtl, or use PR with its k_ij. So PR with its k_ij stays the one that runs; the rule needs an NRTL set for each such pair (docs/DATA_WANTED.md).

PR is the method here: Carbon dioxide, Hydrogen, Carbon monoxide, Nitrogen are light gases, which only an equation of state describes (gas-phase reactors and high-pressure loops are simulated so). Above 10 bar the gE rule (MHV1) would suit, but it has no set here. PR at 7000 kPa, a light gas with a polar liquid (Carbon dioxide + Methanol, Carbon dioxide + Water, Hydrogen + Methanol, Hydrogen + Water, Carbon monoxide + Methanol, Carbon monoxide + Water, Nitrogen + Methanol, Nitrogen + Water): above about 10 bar the method guide recommends a cubic equation with a gE mixing rule (rule 4 of docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md). CHEPTA's rule of that kind would be refused: PR + gE (MHV1): Methanol + Nitrogen, a light gas with a polar liquid, has no NRTL parameters fitted inside the rule (src/data/mhv1.json) and none in the databank, so its solubility would rest on no data (proposal 0018). Pairs fitted so far: carbon-dioxide + methanol, hydrogen + methanol, carbon-monoxide + methanol, methane + methanol, carbon-dioxide + water, hydrogen + water, carbon-monoxide + water, methane + water. Give the pair's NRTL parameters in mixing.nrtl, or use PR with its k_ij. So PR with its k_ij stays the one that runs; the rule needs an NRTL set for each such pair (docs/DATA_WANTED.md).

PR is the method here: Carbon dioxide, Hydrogen, Carbon monoxide, Nitrogen are light gases, which only an equation of state describes (gas-phase reactors and high-pressure loops are simulated so). For a liquid of the polar components alone (Methanol, Water) below about 10 bar, such as their distillation, an activity model (NRTL or UNIQUAC) would be more accurate (docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md).

Above 10 bar the gE rule (MHV1) would suit, but it has no set here. PR at 7000 kPa, a light gas with a polar liquid (Carbon dioxide + Methanol, Carbon dioxide + Water, Hydrogen + Methanol, Hydrogen + Water, Carbon monoxide + Methanol, Carbon monoxide + Water, Nitrogen + Methanol, Nitrogen + Water): above about 10 bar the method guide recommends a cubic equation with a gE mixing rule (rule 4 of docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md). CHEPTA's rule of that kind would be refused: PR + gE (MHV1): Methanol + Nitrogen, a light gas with a polar liquid, has no NRTL parameters fitted inside the rule (src/data/mhv1.json) and none in the databank, so its solubility would rest on no data (proposal 0018). Pairs fitted so far: carbon-dioxide + methanol, hydrogen + methanol, carbon-monoxide + methanol, methane + methanol, carbon-dioxide + water, hydrogen + water, carbon-monoxide + water, methane + water. Give the pair's NRTL parameters in mixing.nrtl, or use PR with its k_ij. So PR with its k_ij stays the one that runs; the rule needs an NRTL set for each such pair (docs/DATA_WANTED.md).

Carbon monoxide: ideal-gas heat capacity at 520.89 K is 20.89 K above its range (68.16-500 K): the record's own equation is evaluated beyond its range (the Aly-Lee form, which follows the molecule's vibrational heat capacity). This is an extrapolation, not data.

PR is the method here: Carbon dioxide, Hydrogen, Carbon monoxide, Nitrogen are light gases, which only an equation of state describes (gas-phase reactors and high-pressure loops are simulated so). For a liquid of the polar components alone (Methanol, Water) below about 10 bar, such as their distillation, an activity model (NRTL or UNIQUAC) would be more accurate (docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md).

Above 10 bar the gE rule (MHV1) would suit, but it has no set here. PR at 1698 kPa, a light gas with a polar liquid (Carbon dioxide + Methanol, Carbon dioxide + Water, Hydrogen + Methanol, Hydrogen + Water, Carbon monoxide + Methanol, Carbon monoxide + Water, Nitrogen + Methanol, Nitrogen + Water): above about 10 bar the method guide recommends a cubic equation with a gE mixing rule (rule 4 of docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md). CHEPTA's rule of that kind would be refused: PR + gE (MHV1): Methanol + Nitrogen, a light gas with a polar liquid, has no NRTL parameters fitted inside the rule (src/data/mhv1.json) and none in the databank, so its solubility would rest on no data (proposal 0018). Pairs fitted so far: carbon-dioxide + methanol, hydrogen + methanol, carbon-monoxide + methanol, methane + methanol, carbon-dioxide + water, hydrogen + water, carbon-monoxide + water, methane + water. Give the pair's NRTL parameters in mixing.nrtl, or use PR with its k_ij. So PR with its k_ij stays the one that runs; the rule needs an NRTL set for each such pair (docs/DATA_WANTED.md).

PR is the method here: Carbon dioxide, Hydrogen, Carbon monoxide, Nitrogen are light gases, which only an equation of state describes (gas-phase reactors and high-pressure loops are simulated so). For a liquid of the polar components alone (Methanol, Water) below about 10 bar, such as their distillation, an activity model (NRTL or UNIQUAC) would be more accurate (docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md).

Above 10 bar the gE rule (MHV1) would suit, but it has no set here. PR at 3000 kPa, a light gas with a polar liquid (Carbon dioxide + Methanol, Carbon dioxide + Water, Hydrogen + Methanol, Hydrogen + Water, Carbon monoxide + Methanol, Carbon monoxide + Water, Nitrogen + Methanol, Nitrogen + Water): above about 10 bar the method guide recommends a cubic equation with a gE mixing rule (rule 4 of docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md). CHEPTA's rule of that kind would be refused: PR + gE (MHV1): Methanol + Nitrogen, a light gas with a polar liquid, has no NRTL parameters fitted inside the rule (src/data/mhv1.json) and none in the databank, so its solubility would rest on no data (proposal 0018). Pairs fitted so far: carbon-dioxide + methanol, hydrogen + methanol, carbon-monoxide + methanol, methane + methanol, carbon-dioxide + water, hydrogen + water, carbon-monoxide + water, methane + water. Give the pair's NRTL parameters in mixing.nrtl, or use PR with its k_ij. So PR with its k_ij stays the one that runs; the rule needs an NRTL set for each such pair (docs/DATA_WANTED.md).

PR is the method here: Carbon dioxide, Hydrogen, Carbon monoxide, Nitrogen are light gases, which only an equation of state describes (gas-phase reactors and high-pressure loops are simulated so). For a liquid of the polar components alone (Methanol, Water) below about 10 bar, such as their distillation, an activity model (NRTL or UNIQUAC) would be more accurate (docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md).

Above 10 bar the gE rule (MHV1) would suit, but it has no set here. PR at 7000 kPa, a light gas with a polar liquid (Carbon dioxide + Methanol, Carbon dioxide + Water, Hydrogen + Methanol, Hydrogen + Water, Carbon monoxide + Methanol, Carbon monoxide + Water, Nitrogen + Methanol, Nitrogen + Water): above about 10 bar the method guide recommends a cubic equation with a gE mixing rule (rule 4 of docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md). CHEPTA's rule of that kind would be refused: PR + gE (MHV1): Methanol + Nitrogen, a light gas with a polar liquid, has no NRTL parameters fitted inside the rule (src/data/mhv1.json) and none in the databank, so its solubility would rest on no data (proposal 0018). Pairs fitted so far: carbon-dioxide + methanol, hydrogen + methanol, carbon-monoxide + methanol, methane + methanol, carbon-dioxide + water, hydrogen + water, carbon-monoxide + water, methane + water. Give the pair's NRTL parameters in mixing.nrtl, or use PR with its k_ij. So PR with its k_ij stays the one that runs; the rule needs an NRTL set for each such pair (docs/DATA_WANTED.md).

PR is the method here: Carbon dioxide, Hydrogen, Carbon monoxide, Nitrogen are light gases, which only an equation of state describes (gas-phase reactors and high-pressure loops are simulated so). For a liquid of the polar components alone (Methanol, Water) below about 10 bar, such as their distillation, an activity model (NRTL or UNIQUAC) would be more accurate (docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md).

Rigorous column: 30 stages (1 the partial condenser, 30 the reboiler), feed on stage 24, at 100 kPa without pressure drop. The MESH equations of every stage were solved together by Newton's method (Naphtali-Sandholm), started by the continuation in the relative volatilities (7 steps), in 17 iterations; every group of residuals is within its tolerance (state.residuals). Converged is not validated against data: the result is as good as the method and its parameters.
No PR k_ij for Carbon dioxide + Carbon monoxide: k_ij = 0 used; results for this pair are a prediction without binary data.
k_ij of Carbon dioxide + Nitrogen (-0.0122) comes from data at 233.15-293.15 K; the stages' 337.51-374.17 K are outside that range.
k_ij of Hydrogen + Carbon monoxide (0.0919) comes from data at 68.2-88.2 K; the stages' 337.51-374.17 K are outside that range.

k_ij of Carbon monoxide + Nitrogen (0.03) comes from data at 70-122 K; the stages' 337.51-374.17 K are outside that range.
No PR k_ij for Water + Nitrogen: k_ij = 0 used; results for this pair are a prediction without binary data.

PR is the method here: Carbon dioxide, Hydrogen, Carbon monoxide, Nitrogen are light gases, which only an equation of state describes (gas-phase reactors and high-pressure loops are simulated so). For a liquid of the polar components alone (Methanol, Water) below about 10 bar, such as their distillation, an activity model (NRTL or UNIQUAC) would be more accurate (docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md).
